function getParameterByName(name, url) {
		if(url == null){
		  url = window.location.href;
		}
	    name = name.replace(/[\[\]]/g, '\\$&');
	    var regex = new RegExp('[?&]' + name + '(=([^&#]*)|&|#|$)'),
		results = regex.exec(url);
	    if (!results) return null;
	    if (!results[2]) return '';
	    return decodeURIComponent(results[2].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
	}

    var STYLE_ID = 'at-body-style';
    function getParent() {
    return doc.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
    }
    function addStyle(parent, id, def) {
        if (!parent) {
        return;
        }
        var style = doc.createElement('style');
        style.id = id;
        style.innerHTML = def;
        parent.appendChild(style);
    }
    function removeStyle(parent, id) {
        if (!parent) {
            return;
        }
        var style = doc.getElementById(id);
        if (!style) {
            return;
        }
        parent.removeChild(style);
    }
    addStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID, style);
    setTimeout(function() {
    removeStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID);
    }, timeout);

		if (Object.prototype.toString.call(str).toLowerCase() === '[object regexp]') {

		}
		// If a string
		return this.replace(new RegExp(str, 'g'), newStr);

	function getCookie(cname) {
	 	var name = cname + "=";
  		var decodedCookie = decodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
		var ca = decodedCookie.split(';');
  		for(var i = 0; i <ca.length; i++) {
    			var c = ca[i];
    			while (c.charAt(0) == ' ') {
     				 c = c.substring(1);
    			}
    			if (c.indexOf(name) == 0) {
    				 return c.substring(name.length, c.length);
    			}
  		}
  		return "";
	}

	var referer = "";//sessionStorage.container;

function callMainSitePrismaNavHTML(){

        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexsearch";

        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=sase&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/sasesearch";

function addStyle(styles) {            
    /* Create style document */
    var css = document.createElement('style');
    css.type = 'text/css';

    if (css.styleSheet) 
        css.styleSheet.cssText = styles;
    else 
        css.appendChild(document.createTextNode(styles));

    /* Append style to the tag name */
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(css);
}
function httpGet(theUrl,req_type) {
    if (window.XMLHttpRequest) { // code for IE7+, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari
        xmlhttp=new XMLHttpRequest();
    } else {// code for IE6, IE5
        xmlhttp=new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
    }
    xmlhttp.onreadystatechange=function()
    {
        if (xmlhttp.readyState==4 && xmlhttp.status==200)
        {
            if(req_type == 'menu_html'){
            var nav_text = xmlhttp.responseText.replaceAll('https://static.cloud.coveo.com/searchui/v2.9159/js/CoveoJsSearch.Lazy.min.js', '');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll('src="/', 'src="'+maindomain_lang+'/');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("'/content", "'"+maindomain_lang+"/content");
                        
            document.getElementById("PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC").innerHTML = nav_text.replaceAll('href="/', 'href="'+maindomain_lang+'/');

            var lozad_back = document.getElementsByClassName('lozad-background');
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(lozad_back, function(el) {
            // Do stuff here
            var el_back_img_path = el.getAttribute('data-background-image');
            var first_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'");
            var last_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'",first_pos+1);
            el_back_img_path = el_back_img_path.substring(first_pos+1,last_pos);
            let result = el_back_img_path.includes(main_site_url);
            if(result == false){
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",main_site_url+el_back_img_path);
            }
            else{
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",el_back_img_path);
            }
            });
            const observer_lozad = lozad('.lozad, .lozad-background'); // lazy loads elements with default selector as '.lozad'
            observer_lozad.observe();
            }
            if(req_type == 'head_inline_css'){
            addStyle(xmlhttp.responseText);
            }
        }
    }
    xmlhttp.open("GET", theUrl, true );
    xmlhttp.send();    
}

    <section class="section blog-contents">

              <div class="be__contents-wrapper">
                <h2><a id="post-176117-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>Unit 42 researchers uncovered a series of cyberespionage campaigns targeting a government organization in Southeast Asia. Our initial investigation began with tracking Stately Taurus activity between June 1–Aug. 15, 2025. This activity involves USB-propagated malware called USBFect (aka HIUPAN), which deploys a PUBLOAD backdoor. Our investigation led to the discovery of two additional, distinct activity clusters we’re tracking as CL-STA-1048 and CL-STA-1049.</p>
<p>The attackers behind CL-STA-1048 used an espionage toolkit comprising several components:</p>
<ul>
<li>EggStremeFuel backdoor</li>
<li>Masol remote access Trojan (RAT)</li>
<li>EggStreme Loader (which delivered the comprehensive Gorem RAT with keylogging)</li>
<li>A simple data theft tool we internally label TrackBak stealer</li>
</ul>
<p>In contrast, CL-STA-1049's operations involved using a novel loader, which we named Hypnosis loader, to deploy the FluffyGh0st RAT payload.</p>
<p>These activity clusters overlap with publicly reported campaigns aimed at establishing persistent access. Significant overlap in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) with known China-aligned campaigns suggests the clusters and threat group have a common target of interest, potentially coordinating their effort.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-url-filtering" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced URL Filtering</a> and <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-security" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced DNS Security</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XDR" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XSIAM" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a></li>
</ul>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>

<h2><a id="post-176117-_gfbps4qqt6ik"></a>Southeast Asian Government Targeting</h2>
<p>This investigation revealed a persistent espionage campaign targeting a government organization in Southeast Asia.</p>
<p>Our analysis identified three distinct clusters of activity in parallel within the victim's network, each with different tools and methods but likely working toward this common objective:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Stately Taurus:</strong> We attributed one of the activity clusters with high confidence to this threat actor, which leveraged USB-based malware to deploy the <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/stately-taurus-uses-bookworm-malware/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PUBLOAD</a> backdoor, a consistent TTP for this group.</li>
<li><strong>CL-STA-1048:</strong> This cluster includes attacks using a toolkit of espionage payloads, deploying multiple RATs like <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/k/earth-estries.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MasolRAT</a> and the RawCookie backdoor. The use of diverse and sometimes noisy tooling suggests a determined effort to establish a foothold. This activity shows links to publicly reported China-affiliated actors like <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/k/earth-estries.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earth Estries</a> and those behind the <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/operation-crimson-palace-sophos-threat-hunting-unveils-multiple-clusters-of-chinese-state-sponsored-activity-targeting-southeast-asia" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Crimson Palace</a> Campaign.</li>
<li><strong>CL-STA-1049:</strong> This cluster features stealth and persistence, with attackers using the novel Hypnosis loader to deploy the FluffyGh0st RAT. This activity overlaps with the China-aligned group known as <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/deep-dive-into-unfading-sea-haze-a-new-threat-actor-in-the-south-china-sea" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unfading Sea Haze.</a></li>
</ul>
<p>The convergence of these three distinct, China-aligned clusters against a single, high-value government target illustrates a complex and well-resourced operation. Figure 1 provides a visual overview of the relationships between these activity clusters, the tools used in the attacks and previously reported threat groups.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176129" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176129" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176129 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1.png" alt="A diagram depicting a network of cyber threats and defenses. Skulls represent threats, while gears and padlocks indicate security measures. Key elements include malware used by the different attackers." width="1000" height="809" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1-544x440.png 544w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1-865x700.png 865w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1-768x621.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-484412-176117-1-1536x1243.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176129" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. An overview of the activity clustering.</figcaption></figure>
<h2><a id="post-176117-_qm30fmmshoqz"></a><strong>Stately Taurus - PUBLOAD Activity</strong></h2>
<p>On June 1, 2025, we detected PUBLOAD activity attributed to Stately Taurus across multiple endpoints at a government entity in Southeast Asia. Our investigation found the origin of this activity was likely a USB drive containing <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/i/earth-preta-new-malware-and-strategies.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">USBFect</a>. USBfect is a worm that spreads via removable media, often used to propagate PUBLOAD for lateral movement.</p>
<p>This malware's functionality is identical to HIUPAN's, documented by <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/i/earth-preta-new-malware-and-strategies.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Trend Micro in 2024</a>. We assess that USBFect and HIUPAN are the same malware family. The USBFect sample analyzed in this activity implemented the following previously observed capabilities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Installing USBFect components onto the infected system</li>
<li>Monitoring for removable or hot-pluggable drive insertion</li>
<li>Copying USBFect components onto a removable or hot-pluggable drive</li>
</ul>
<p>However, this USBFect sample has an overt PDB filepath: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">D:\WorkProject\2023\GJ0215\src\USBInfection\sln\USBFect\Release\USBFect.pdb</span>.</p>
<p>We found evidence of USBFect infection in multiple agents with the following path: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">D:\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\EVENT.dll</span>.</p>
<p>The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">EVENT.dll</span> file has the following SHA256 hash:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">4b29b74798a4e6538f2ba245c57be82953383dc91fe0a91b984b903d12043e92</span></li>
</ul>
<p>This malware is a variant of <a href="https://0x0d4y.blog/mustang-panda-employ-publoader-through-claimloader-yes-another-dll-side-loading-technique-delivery-via-phishing/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ClaimLoader</a>, which is embedded in the generated drive path and responsible for loading PUBLOAD into memory. We observed this propagation to multiple endpoints until Aug. 15, 2025, at 00:17:15 UTC.</p>
<p>Endpoints with PUBLOAD malware also used the following file paths:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ProgramData/intel/_/$.ini</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ProgramData/Intel/_/EVENT.dll</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ProgramData/intel/_/u2ec.dll</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ProgramData/intel/_/UsbConfig.exe</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Libraries\Dialogui\EVENT.dll</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The malware stages these files to execute and propagate its payload via USB devices.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_hqxw3fijjrno"></a><strong>ClaimLoader</strong></h3>
<p>ClaimLoader (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">EVENT.dll</span>) is a shellcode loader, documented by Japanese IT security company <a href="https://www.lac.co.jp/lacwatch/report/20221117_003189.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">LAC in 2022</a>, that loads the PUBLOAD backdoor in memory. The sample identified in this activity largely had the same capabilities, but with slight variations. The malware copies its components to a working directory (e.g., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Users\Public\Libraries\Dialogui</span>). These components include:</p>
<ul>
<li>A legitimate parent process</li>
<li>ClaimLoader itself</li>
</ul>
<p>The loader then registers the copied legitimate application in a Windows registry autorun key to establish persistence.</p>
<p>ClaimLoader then uses an XOR key to decrypt an embedded shellcode payload and executes the shellcode by using the CryptEnumOIDInfo API. This technique, shown below in Figure 2, is similar to the one described in LAC’s report.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176140" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176140" style="width: 700px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176140 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-487510-176117-2.png" alt="Code snippet displaying a function that decodes and runs shellcode. The code uses functions like &#96;strcpy&#96;, &#96;VirtualAlloc&#96;, &#96;memcpy&#96;, and &#96;CryptEnumOIDInfo&#96;. It comments on decoding the shellcode by XOR and running the shellcode via Callback." width="700" height="284" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-487510-176117-2.png 1180w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-487510-176117-2-786x318.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-487510-176117-2-768x311.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 700px) 100vw, 700px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176140" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. Shellcode decryption and execution by ClaimLoader.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The shellcode is PUBLOAD, first documented by <a href="https://blog.talosintelligence.com/mustang-panda-targets-europe/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cisco Talos in 2022</a>. Variants of PUBLOAD use either HTTP or TCP for command-and-control (C2) communications. The sample we observed is a variant that uses TCP.</p>
<p>PUBLOAD encrypts data from the infected host, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Volume info</li>
<li>Computer name</li>
<li>Username</li>
<li>Tick count</li>
</ul>
<p>The malware accomplishes this by using multiple XOR loops and sends the information with a fake TLS header (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">17 03 03</span>) over TCP.</p>
<p>Once PUBLOAD receives a response from the C2 server, it decodes and executes the final payload in memory. During our analysis, we did not identify any further stages of tooling.</p>
<p>In November 2024, we analyzed similar activity from Stately Taurus, including an identical <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/4b29b74798a4e6538f2ba245c57be82953383dc91fe0a91b984b903d12043e92/detection" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PUBLOAD sample</a>. This sample maintained consistent configurations and aligned with <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/i/earth-preta-new-malware-and-strategies.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Trend Micro's research</a> on the group.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_8pwzuq7mfoqc"></a><strong>CoolClient</strong></h3>
<p>During the same time period, on Aug. 4, 2025, at 08:50:15 UTC, we detected the two suspicious DLL files listed in Table 1 on an agent without PUBLOAD activity.</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>SHA256</b></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>File Path</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">835795aa494021752f21fbef63c81227c1b934437a02aa1f2a258c9f60b0b7a3</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\ProgramData\GoogleUpdate\libvlc.dll</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">851d57a2bf514202f54dafa1eb83a862653be7512b6e9535914b8d1d719d495f</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Users\$USER$\AppData\LocalLow\Brother\PrtDrv\sangforvpnlibcrypto-1_1.dll</span></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 1. CoolClient loader DLL files.</span></p>
<p>Our analysis of the samples revealed they were CoolClient loaders. CoolClient loader is a shellcode loader that heavily implements anti-disassembly techniques. Without countering these techniques, analysis tools can produce incorrectly disassembled code, as shown in Figure 3 below.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176151" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176151" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176151 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-489573-176117-3.png" alt="The image displays a disassembled code snippet, showing a series of hexadecimal addresses and instructions. " width="900" height="1083" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-489573-176117-3.png 1256w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-489573-176117-3-366x440.png 366w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-489573-176117-3-581x700.png 581w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-489573-176117-3-768x925.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176151" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. An incorrectly disassembled CoolClient loader due to anti-disassembly techniques.</figcaption></figure>
<p>These DLL files load payloads from an encrypted file located at:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">c:\programdata\GoogleUpdate\loader.ja</span></li>
</ul>
<p>We were unable to obtain this file during our investigation. However, it likely overlaps with the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">loader.ja</span> file <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/c/earth-preta-updated-stealthy-strategies.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reported by Trend Micro</a> that loads the final CoolClient payload.</p>
<p>CoolClient was first reported by <a href="https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2022/11/03/family-tree-dll-sideloading-cases-may-be-related/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Sophos in 2022</a> and observed in Stately Taurus activity by <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/c/earth-preta-updated-stealthy-strategies.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Trend Micro in 2023</a>. This threat is built on the open-source C++ library HP-Socket to support multiple C2 protocols and a client/server two-way connection. Figure 4 shows HP-Socket's class information embedded in a CoolClient sample.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176162" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176162" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176162 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4.png" alt="Diagram illustrating similarities between class structures. The top half shows embedded class information with a highlighted section in red, linking to the bottom half which displays an identical class structure to HP-Socket's source code." width="1000" height="766" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4.png 1758w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4-575x440.png 575w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4-914x700.png 914w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4-768x588.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-494413-176117-4-1536x1176.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176162" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. HP-Socket’s class information embedded in CoolClient.</figcaption></figure>
<p>CoolClient supports the following capabilities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Uploading and deleting a file</li>
<li>Tunneling packets</li>
<li>Starting keylogging</li>
<li>Sending port map information</li>
</ul>
<p>The lack of arbitrary code execution in CoolClient suggests it is designed as a tunneling tool or stealer that attackers could use to gather information for further lateral movement.</p>
<p>CoolClient activity was distinct from PUBLOAD infections. However, we confirmed that the specific anti-disassembly technique used by the CoolClient loader samples we found is identical to that used by USBFect/HIUPAN. This supports our attribution of CoolClient activity to Stately Taurus, suggesting it was another attempt by the group to secure access.</p>
<h2><a id="post-176117-_krah8084rfk"></a>CL-STA-1048 - Espionage Toolkit</h2>
<p>The activity, tracked under CL-STA-1048, deployed a wide variety of tools with similar functionality. This pattern suggests that the threat actor behind CL-STA-1048 actively sought a payload that could bypass XDR. In the process of doing so, they inadvertently exposed a significant portion of their toolkit to our analysis.</p>
<p>On Aug. 9, 2025, we observed alerts originating from a Microsoft Edge process. Our investigation of this alert identified a DLL named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">mscorsvc.dll</span> (SHA256: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">1aa37a477c539edf25656a300002a28d4246ec83344422dd705b42d3443a2623</span>) being loaded into memory via mscorsvw.exe.</p>
<p>We identified this DLL as a lightweight, TCP-based backdoor written in C, which we determined was <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/eggstreme-fileless-malware-cyberattack-apac" target="_blank" rel="noopener">EggStremeFuel</a>. While the initial execution vector for EggStremeFuel remains unknown, the subsequent activity was highly revealing, including the attempted deployment of several tools.</p>
<p>The following sections detail our analysis of these tools, starting with the initial identification of EggStremeFuel.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_y2mwuz8l1sg4"></a><strong>EggStremeFuel</strong></h3>
<p>During its initialization, EggStremeFuel encrypts embedded C2 configurations using RC4 and stores them in <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Cookies\Cookies.dat</span>.</p>
<p>The configuration is structured as a key-value pair separated by two pound (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">#</span>) symbols. An example of this is shown below:</p>
<p style="padding-left: 40px;"><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">dm:laichingte[.]net##ip:58.69.38[.]83##st:30##mp:443##mp:443##bp:5228##</span></p>
<p>EggStremeFuel imports this C2 configuration from <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Cookies.dat</span> upon each execution, allowing for dynamic updates. It then starts its C2 communication with an initial check-in, sending the C2 server a random 16-byte session key and its MD5 hash.</p>
<p>The backdoor then encrypts and decrypts all C2 communication using RC4 with this session key. The backdoor supports the following capabilities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Uploading or downloading files</li>
<li>Listing files or directories</li>
<li>Starting or terminating a reverse shell</li>
<li>Sending the current global IP address</li>
<li>Getting, updating or overwriting the C2 configuration</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_wu9r3ua9nxo2"></a><strong>Masol RAT</strong></h3>
<p>Twenty minutes after we observed the EggStremeFuel deployment, Cortex XDR detected another malicious payload on the same agent at the following path <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Windows\System32\AxInstSVs.dll</span> (SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">05995284b59ad0066350f43517382228f7eee63cd297e787b2a271f69ecf2dfc</span>). We identified the second sample as Masol RAT, an HTTP-based Windows backdoor previously documented by <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/crimson-palace-new-tools-tactics-targets" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Sophos</a> and <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/k/earth-estries.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Trend Micro</a> in 2024.</p>
<p>The sample recovered during this incident contained an embedded program database (PDB) path identical to the one Sophos and Trend Micro referenced: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">E:\Masol_https190228\x64\Release\Masol.pdb</span>.</p>
<p>Masol RAT also has several overlaps with the Linux backdoor known as Backdr-NQ, which <a href="https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2022/10/19/covert-channels/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Sophos reported in 2022</a>. Both backdoors share a similar code flow, the same configuration decryption algorithm and the same backdoor commands.</p>
<p>The Masol RAT we observed in this incident is designed to be executed as a Windows service DLL and is not packed or obfuscated.</p>
<p>It communicates with its C2 servers over HTTP POST, encrypted by AES. Masol RAT features backdoor commands for the following activities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Executing arbitrary commands</li>
<li>Getting or updating C2 configurations</li>
<li>Uploading or downloading a file</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_mhmfruotp38h"></a><strong>EggStreme Loader</strong></h3>
<p>Concurrent with the deployment of Masol RAT, we detected other malware identified as <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/eggstreme-fileless-malware-cyberattack-apac" target="_blank" rel="noopener">EggStreme loader</a> (aka EggStreme Agent or Gorem RAT) at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Windows\System32\XblAuthManagers.dll</span> (SHA256: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">6caa78943939bd7518f5e7eaa44fa778d0db8b822e260d7fe281cf45513f82d9</span>). This finding aligns with <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/eggstreme-fileless-malware-cyberattack-apac" target="_blank" rel="noopener">a Bitdefender blog post</a> detailing similar activity in Southeast Asia.</p>
<p>EggStreme loader is a multi-layered loader designed to launch a payload, Gorem RAT. EggStreme loader leverages multiple publicly available tools, such as <a href="https://github.com/bats3c/DarkLoadLibrary" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DarkLoadLibrary</a> and <a href="https://github.com/hasherezade/libpeconv" target="_blank" rel="noopener">libpeconv</a>, to achieve an in-memory payload execution. Although Cortex XDR prevented the final payload from executing, our analysis suggests attackers attempted to deploy Gorem RAT, shown below in Figure 5.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176173" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176173" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176173 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5.png" alt="Flowchart illustrating a malware process involving EggStreme Loader. It includes elements like &quot;DarkLoadLibrary,&quot; a MUI file, and an EXE file. The chart shows the decryption and injection stages leading to the Gorem RAT (EXE) through DLL injection. It highlights various stages of encrypted data processes." width="1000" height="489" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5-786x385.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5-1431x700.png 1431w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5-768x376.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-497751-176117-5-1536x752.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176173" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. An overview of EggStreme Loader’s execution flow.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This malware uses Google Remote Procedure Call (gRPC) for C2 communication. This method provides the malware with a wide array of functionalities through its backdoor commands. Furthermore, it acts as a launcher for a user-mode keylogger module.</p>
<p>The keylogger module performs the following activities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Capturing keystrokes, window titles, clipboard contents and network information</li>
<li>Saving the output to the following path:<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"> %LOCALAPPDATA%\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Explorer\\thumbcache.dat</span></li>
</ul>
<p>Gorem RAT incorporates a total of 59 backdoor commands, enabling various functionalities. Most backdoor commands are identical to the command Bitdefender reported. However, we observed a variant of Gorem RAT that implements a new feature to upload or download over Dropbox.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_1hcx4plk4u5v"></a><strong>TrackBak</strong></h3>
<p>Finally, 40 minutes after the attackers attempted to deploy Masol RAT, we observed a malicious payload we have named TrackBak based on its log output filename. This payload masquerades as an MS Edge log file to track user activity history. (SHA256: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">84e37e42312b9a502c40cf1f3fc181e3ebd4f3e35c58bbf182740dfe38d3b6b9</span>)</p>
<p>TrackBak is an infostealer that performs the following activities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Collecting key logs</li>
<li>Exfiltrating clipboard data</li>
<li>Gathering network information</li>
<li>Collecting files from drives</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_fefsf422exk9"></a><strong>Attribution</strong></h3>
<p>There are a number of links between CL-STA-1048 and China-affiliated activity. In particular, the use of both <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/k/earth-estries.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Masol RAT</a> and <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/eggstreme-fileless-malware-cyberattack-apac" target="_blank" rel="noopener">EggStreme</a> was publicly reported in relation to China-affiliated activity, such as <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/crimson-palace-new-tools-tactics-targets" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Crimson Palace</a> and <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/24/k/earth-estries.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earth Estries</a>.</p>
<p>Chinese threat groups often share tooling, as well as tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) with each other. As such, we cannot state with certainty whether these public reports relate to the same group.</p>
<h2><a id="post-176117-_6r0fw5l15pyh"></a>CL-STA-1049 - Stealthy Loader and FluffyGh0st RAT Deployment</h2>
<p>On Aug. 1, 2025, we identified yet another cluster of activity, which we track as CL-STA-1049. The attackers deployed a novel DLL loader to install <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/deep-dive-into-unfading-sea-haze-a-new-threat-actor-in-the-south-china-sea" target="_blank" rel="noopener">FluffyGh0st RAT</a>. We named this malware Hypnosis loader.</p>
<p>FluffyGh0st RAT is associated with <a href="https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/businessinsights/deep-dive-into-unfading-sea-haze-a-new-threat-actor-in-the-south-china-sea" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unfading Sea Haze</a> and overlaps with activity tracked by Sophos as <a href="https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2024/06/05/operation-crimson-palace-sophos-threat-hunting-unveils-multiple-clusters-of-chinese-state-sponsored-activity-targeting-southeast-asia/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Crimson Palace</a>.</p>
<p>Starting on Aug. 1, 2025, Cortex XDR generated multiple alerts related to suspicious files in the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Program Files\Common Files\Bitdefender\SetupInformation\</span> directory.</p>
<p>These alerts highlighted a DLL sideloading attack that used a legitimate Bitdefender executable, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">seccenter.exe</span>. Alerts focused on three files associated with the Hypnosis loader activity that were dropped in the Bitdefender application directory are shown in Table 2.</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>SHA256 Hash</b></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>File Path</b></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>Malware</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">9d7c8d3bc4ac108fb2602424a1f4918c051c2443f0526bbb2c970c8e57dbd90d</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">C:\Program Files\Common Files\Bitdefender\SetupInformation\version.dll</span></td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">c774fd7373084f93383593f0a40f56c8a8b95b73e59cd4fc7117daa6b7441e73</span></td>

<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 2. Identified samples of malware from the Hypnosis loader activity.</span></p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_5q6ssv2o1wr"></a><strong>Hypnosis Loader</strong></h3>
<p>Our analysis revealed that the malicious Hypnosis loader DLL is sideloaded by <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">seccenter.exe</span>. To prevent the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">seccenter.exe</span> application that sideloaded the malicious Hypnosis loader DLL from crashing, all the DLL's exported functions are proxied to the legitimate <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">version.dll</span> file located in the Windows system directory.</p>
<p>Once side-loaded by the EXE, Hypnosis loader patches the DLL's host process entry point, redirecting execution to an infinite <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Sleep</span> function. This ensures the main thread does not terminate while the malicious routine executes later, as shown in Figures 6 and 7.</p>
<figure id="attachment_176184" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176184" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176184 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-501446-176117-6.png" alt="Screenshot of a code snippet with hex values. It includes calls to VirtualProtect and calculations involving memory addresses and offsets." width="1000" height="119" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-501446-176117-6.png 1476w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-501446-176117-6-786x94.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-501446-176117-6-768x92.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176184" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. Hypnosis loader’s code to patch the DLL's host process entry point.</figcaption></figure>
<figure id="attachment_176195" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-176195" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-176195 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-503599-176117-7.png" alt="Code comparison image highlighting differences between &quot;before patch&quot; and &quot;after patch&quot; sections on the left, and a &quot;jump&quot; point leading to an &quot;infinite loop&quot; section on the right." width="1000" height="305" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-503599-176117-7.png 1884w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-503599-176117-7-786x239.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-503599-176117-7-768x234.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/word-image-503599-176117-7-1536x468.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-176195" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. Disassembled instructions showing the patched DLL host process code.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After patching the DLL's host process, Hypnosis loader creates a new thread to decrypt the name of the final payload (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span>) with an RC4 key and loads it using the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">LoadLibrary</span> API.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_rkwgikj6cal"></a><strong>Initial Analysis of the Final Payload</strong></h3>
<p>Based on our analysis of Hypnosis loader (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">version.dll</span>), the file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span> is likely the final payload. However, we could not recover this sample. Our telemetry revealed the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span> file communicated with a server at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">webmail.rpcthai[.]com</span>. The base domain <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">rpcthai[.]com</span> appears to be used for the website of a legitimate Thai-based company, which implies that attackers hijacked the domain and created <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">webmail.rpcthai[.]com</span> to act as a C2 server.</p>
<p>Looking for other related samples communicating to this domain, we found a DLL file with the SHA256 hash <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">34bf325492614dd4d842ec24f22a402ab73908cb91a74846945eae4775290ff2</span>. This DLL's imphash value <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0bf0bd027fda34d4afa5f86b6340019</span> leads to two payloads on VirusTotal uploaded in 2024:</p>
<ul>
<li>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/f07b2af21e3fab6af5166a44ca77ed0ebc7c9a3e623202a63d4c4492abce8d65" target="_blank" rel="noopener">f07b2af21e3fab6af5166a44ca77ed0ebc7c9a3e623202a63d4c4492abce8d65</a></span></li>
<li>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/58ed0463d4cb393cd09198a6409591b39cae06bb0ba5f5d760186de88410f6b8" target="_blank" rel="noopener">58ed0463d4cb393cd09198a6409591b39cae06bb0ba5f5d760186de88410f6b8</a></span></li>
</ul>
<p>Our analysis revealed that these payloads were FluffyGh0st. Sophos referenced the second sample in a report on a <a href="https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2024/09/10/crimson-palace-new-tools-tactics-targets/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chinese espionage campaign called Crimson Palace</a>.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_p1zzwojdqm68"></a><strong>$FILE_NAME$.log and Its Relationship to the Final Payload</strong></h3>
<p>The file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">$FILE_NAME$.log</span> is a DLL file. Advanced WildFire analysis revealed this DLL file has an embedded network configuration pointing to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">webmail.homesmountain[.]com</span>, which matches the domain structure of the C2 server that the likely final payload <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span> communicated with.</p>
<p>With its imphash value <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">511898b2f71f31932dfb3ee06e904289</span>, we identified additional samples that we also attributed to FluffyGh0st:</p>
<ul>
<li>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/4e26aa1bb28874f0897ab9a08e61d4b99caaa395fe63cbe4398f7297371e388c" target="_blank" rel="noopener">4e26aa1bb28874f0897ab9a08e61d4b99caaa395fe63cbe4398f7297371e388c</a></span></li>
<li>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/4e26aa1bb28874f0897ab9a08e61d4b99caaa395fe63cbe4398f7297371e388c" target="_blank" rel="noopener">11c7728697d5ea11c592fee213063c6369340051157f71ddc7ca891f5f367720</a></span></li>
</ul>
<p>The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">11c7728697d5ea11c592fee213063c6369340051157f71ddc7ca891f5f367720</span> sample is contained in a <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/c47d55ad95a6c6ffac45c2b205e03bddadf5e36f55988599053b1fd0e49448a5" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ZIP archive file that was submitted to VirusTotal</a>. This ZIP archive also contained a <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/8781f2d85eec49205b29aa4bc09b1d7d1dd9e1a650634393e3adbc5354738a51" target="_blank" rel="noopener">sample of Hypnosis loader</a>.</p>
<p>Given the overlaps of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span> with FluffyGh0st and our discovery of the ZIP archive with both Hypnosis loader and FluffyGh0st, it is plausible that the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">bdusersy.dll</span> discovered is FluffyGh0st.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_34mzb0ugpoip"></a><strong>FluffyGh0st</strong></h3>
<p>FluffyGh0st is a custom version of the publicly available Gh0st RAT, which <a href="https://blogapp.bitdefender.com/labs/content/files/2024/05/Bitdefender-Report-DeepDive-creat7721-en_EN.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Bitdefender first reported in 2024 [PDF]</a>. Bitdefender attributed this malware to a China-aligned threat actor that they call Unfading Sea Haze.</p>
<p>FluffyGh0st is designed to allow the attacker to manipulate the system via remote access, but its full capabilities require additional plugins. It downloads these plugins from C2 servers embedded in the sample, which are encrypted with RC4 and compressed using LZNT1, before attempting to execute the export function InstallPlugin.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_pbcqq89sfwv9"></a><strong>Attribution</strong></h3>
<p>Although we did not observe direct evidence linking CL-STA-1049 with CL-STA-1048 during this incident, these clusters may be part of the Crimson Palace campaign. CL-STA-1049 is likely associated with the group Bitdefender called Unfading Sea Haze, and some of its tooling overlaps with <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/operation-crimson-palace-sophos-threat-hunting-unveils-multiple-clusters-of-chinese-state-sponsored-activity-targeting-southeast-asia" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cluster Bravo of Crimson Palace</a>. CL-STA-1048 is potentially linked to <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/operation-crimson-palace-sophos-threat-hunting-unveils-multiple-clusters-of-chinese-state-sponsored-activity-targeting-southeast-asia" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cluster Charlie of Crimson Palace,</a> based on its use of FluffyGh0st.</p>
<h2><a id="post-176117-_2an8ryq91inv"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>Between June and August 2025, attackers targeted a Southeast Asian government entity with a persistent cyberespionage campaign involving three distinct clusters of activity. One cluster we've attributed to Stately Taurus, and the other two we have designated as CL-STA-1048 and CL-STA-1049. The convergence of these activity clusters, all of which show links to known China-aligned actors, points to a coordinated effort to achieve a common strategic goal.</p>
<p>The attackers' methodology indicates they intended to gain long-term, persistent access to sensitive government networks, not just to cause disruption. These well-resourced adversaries used diverse tool sets, including Stately Taurus's USB propagation, CL-STA-1048's multi-payload strategy and CL-STA-1049's stealthy FluffyGh0st RAT. Their primary goal was to continuously locate and exfiltrate data, as evidenced by the deployment of infostealers and comprehensive backdoors.</p>
<h3><a id="post-176117-_lsbythhc3nz9"></a><strong>Palo Alto Networks Protection and Mitigation</strong></h3>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li>The <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a> machine-learning models and analysis techniques have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.</li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-url-filtering" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced URL Filtering</a> and <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-security" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced DNS Security</a> identify known domains and URLs associated with this activity as malicious.</li>
<li><a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XDR" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XSIAM" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a> can help prevent the threats described in this article by employing the <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XDR/Cortex-XDR-4.x-Documentation/Malware-protection" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Malware Prevention Engine</a>. This approach combines several layers of protection, including <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a>, Behavioral Threat Protection and the Local Analysis module, designed to prevent both known and unknown malware from causing harm to endpoints.</li>
</ul>
<p>If you think you may have been compromised or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a> or call:</p>
<ul>
<li>North America: Toll Free: +1 (866) 486-4842 (866.4.UNIT42)</li>
<li>UK: +44.20.3743.3660</li>
<li>Europe and Middle East: +31.20.299.3130</li>
<li>Asia: +65.6983.8730</li>
<li>Japan: +81.50.1790.0200</li>
<li>Australia: +61.2.4062.7950</li>
<li>India: 000 800 050 45107</li>
<li>South Korea: +82.080.467.8774</li>
</ul>
<p>Palo Alto Networks has shared these findings with our fellow Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) members. CTA members use this intelligence to rapidly deploy protections to their customers and to systematically disrupt malicious cyber actors. Learn more about the <a href="https://www.cyberthreatalliance.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cyber Threat Alliance</a>.</p>

                    <h4 class="post-title">Threat Brief: March 2026 Escalation of Cyber Risk Related to Iran (Updated March 26)</h4>
                  </a>

<script>
 var PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE = 'en_US';

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
        var isCaptchaComplete02  = false;	
        window.captchaInlineFormOnload = function(token){
            isCaptchaComplete02 = true;
            $("form[name='Unit42_Subscribe'] button[id='unit42footerSubscription_form_button']").prop('disabled', false);
        }
        var PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = false;
        const SITE_KEY = '6LdDKhIsAAAAABdoYV3PR5VJ2Gz23_dLSvq2uvBQ'; 
                if(!PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED){
               PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = true;
               // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
               var recapthaScript = $("script[src='https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload']").length
               // console.log("recapthaScript",recapthaScript);
               if (!recapthaScript) {
                   var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                   var script = document.createElement('script');
                   script.typerecapthaScript = 'text/javascript';
                   script.src = "https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload";
                   head.appendChild(script);
               }
               else{
                   captchaInlineFormOnload();
                }
           }
            	
	
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		

		if (success) {
                                                if(grecaptcha){
                        grecaptcha.enterprise.ready(function() {
                            grecaptcha.enterprise.execute(SITE_KEY, {action: 'submit'}).then(function(token) {
                                submitSubscribeForm({token :token, action : 'submit'},form);
                            });
                        });
                    }
                    			
		}
		return false;
	});
        function submitSubscribeForm(tokenData, form){
            var serialized_data = form.serialize();
            let captchaParams = `&g-recaptcha-response=${tokenData.token}&action=${tokenData.action}`;
            $.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: serialized_data+captchaParams,
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
            
        }
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});
</script>

	var isProcessing = false; 
    function alter_ul_post_values(obj,post_id,ul_type){
	
		if (isProcessing)    
		return;  
		isProcessing = true;   
		var like_nonce = jQuery('#_wpnonce').val();
		jQuery(obj).find("span").html("..");
                jQuery.ajax({
                    type: "POST",
                    url: "https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/plugins/like-dislike-counter-for-posts-pages-and-comments/ajax_counter.php",
                    data: "post_id="+post_id+"&up_type="+ul_type+"&ul_nonce="+like_nonce,
                    success: function(msg){
                            jQuery(obj).find("span").html(msg);
                            isProcessing = false; 
                            jQuery(obj).find('svg').children('path').attr('stroke','#0050FF');
                            jQuery(obj).removeClass('idc_ul_cont_not_liked idc_ul_cont_not_liked_inner');
                    }
 		});
	}

function noSell(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
   if (( typeof OneTrust != 'undefined') &&  (!!OneTrust)) {
       OneTrust.ToggleInfoDisplay();
    }else{
      var href = event.target.getAttribute('href');
        window.open(href, '_blank'); 
    }
}

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}
if(referer == "CloudCortex" || referer == "Prisma" || referer == "Cortex" || referer == "Sase" || referer == "Unit" || referer == "Ngfw"){

      loadScript(main_site_criticalTopBase, false);

      loadScript1(main_site_critical_top, function(){
        window.PAN_initializeProduct2021Nav();
      });
      loadScript(main_site_defered, false);
    }, 3000);
	}
}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};
